PyRIT wraps the real HTTP/SDK error behind a generic "Error sending prompt" message, so you can't see what's actually failing. Two likely causes: `OpenAIChatTarget`'s `endpoint` needs the full Azure deployment path plus api-version, not just the bare resource URL your working AzureOpenAI code uses; and the model argument needs to be the *deployment name*, passed via `model_name`.

```python
target = OpenAIChatTarget(
    endpoint="https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/<deployment>/chat/completions?api-version=2024-02-01",
    api_key="myApiKey",
    model_name="myModel",  # the Azure *deployment* name, not the base model
)
```

Also enable logging before calling `send_prompts_async` — PyRIT logs the underlying exception (real status code/reason) at DEBUG level, which the printed conversation-ID error hides:

```python
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG)
```

That will surface the actual 4xx/5xx response instead of the wrapped generic error, telling you exactly which part of the request Azure is rejecting.

Your analysis is right: this is I/O-bound blocking work over a mostly-synchronous hardware API, so a thread-per-DUT model is the pragmatic choice over asyncio. Rewriting your serial driver to be async-native is a lot of work for little gain when the real concurrency need is simply "many blocking waits happening at once."

Use `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` with one worker per DUT (or one `threading.Thread` each), and protect any shared, non-thread-safe resource (DB/server connections, shared hardware) with a `threading.Lock`, or a bounded `threading.Semaphore` if several DUTs may share it but not unlimited concurrently:

```python
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(duts)) as ex:
    futures = [ex.submit(run_test, dut) for dut in duts]
```

Write each DUT's test as an ordinary sequential function — the executor gives you cross-DUT parallelism for free without touching your serial code. If you later scale to hundreds of DUTs, asyncio with `loop.run_in_executor` wrapping the blocking serial calls is a valid hybrid, but for typical bench setups threads are simpler and avoid rewriting your driver. Skip multiprocessing — no CPU-bound work here.

This is a version-mismatch bug, not something in your code. `geopandas.plotting._flatten_multi_geoms` was a private helper that got removed when geopandas reworked its plotting internals (around 0.10+), but `geovoronoi.plotting` still imports it directly, so the import fails against modern geopandas.

Fix by pinning an older, compatible geopandas:

```bash
pip install "geopandas<0.10" descartes
```

Better long-term fix: stop relying on `geovoronoi.plotting` (it's effectively unmaintained against current geopandas) and plot the polygons yourself, since `voronoi_regions_from_coords` already returns shapely polygons you can wrap directly:

```python
import geopandas as gpd
gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=list(region_polys.values()))
ax = gdf.plot(edgecolor="black", facecolor="none")
```

Also note `cascaded_union` is deprecated/removed in newer shapely (use `unary_union` only) and `descartes` is unmaintained, so avoiding the whole `geovoronoi.plotting` + `descartes` stack is more future-proof than just downgrading geopandas.

Those `[0m`/`[1m`-style sequences are raw ANSI color/reset escape codes. SeleniumBase sets up colored console logging on import, and whatever "Shell window" you're printing into doesn't interpret ANSI codes, so you see the literal escape text instead of colors.

Options:

1. Run from a terminal that does support ANSI (Windows Terminal, VS Code's integrated terminal, a modern cmd/PowerShell) — there they'll render as actual colors instead of text.
2. Silence SeleniumBase's own logger instead of relying on env toggles:

```python
import logging
logging.getLogger("seleniumbase").setLevel(logging.WARNING)
```

3. If your IDE's console has an "enable ANSI/color passthrough" setting (e.g. Spyder → Preferences → IPython console), turning that on fixes the display without touching your code.

The key point: it's not a bug in your script, it's a mismatch between SeleniumBase emitting color codes and your output pane not rendering them — switching the console you run in is the most reliable fix.

No — scraping the HTML can't give you the PHP source or server-side logic, because PHP runs entirely on the server before the response is sent; the client (and your scraper) only ever sees whatever that script *outputs*, never its code.

What you can get is the rendered content of `ML_print_value.php` itself, by requesting the iframe's `src` URL directly (resolved against the page's base URL):

```python
import requests
url = "https://example.com/ML_print_value.php?p=DFT_bandgap_HF&f=321227475&u=eV&sd=1&mod=_aTbTme"
r = requests.get(url)
print(r.text)
```

That returns whatever HTML/text the script renders (presumably the formatted numeric value shown in the iframe) — that's the only "PHP information" externally accessible. Missing here: the real domain/base URL, so the exact request can't be confirmed; if the endpoint needs a session/referrer, copy those headers from your browser's Network tab.

`ld: cannot find -lz` means the linker can't locate `libz.so`/`libz.a`, even though zlib is "installed" — in a conda env this usually means the shared library isn't actually present under that specific env's `lib/`, or the linker just isn't searching it. Fix by installing zlib into the active conda env itself:

```bash
conda activate py37
conda install -c conda-forge zlib
```

That puts `libz.so` under `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib`. If it's already there and linking still fails, point the linker at it explicitly before building:

```bash
export LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib:$LIBRARY_PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
make install
```

Since you're using the conda-provided compiler (`x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-cc`), it normally searches `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` automatically, so the most likely gap is simply that this env's zlib package (with the actual `.so`, not just headers pulled in as another package's dependency) was never installed.

"Internal Server Error" coming back means the request reaching the server differs from what Postman sends — almost always the body. Your `payload` is a Python string containing literal `\r\n` escape characters (pasted from Postman's generated snippet), which is fragile and error-prone to hand-build as JSON text.

Don't construct JSON as a raw string — build a dict and let `requests` serialize it:

```python
import requests
payload = {"startDate": "2000-12-25", "endDate": "2000-12-31", "format": "CSV"}
headers = {"authorization": "Bearer XXXXX", "content-type": "application/json"}
r = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers)
print(r.status_code, r.text)
```

Using `json=` sets `Content-Type`/encoding correctly and eliminates the escaping bug. If it still 500s, compare the exact bytes Postman sends (Postman Console → raw request) against what `requests` sends — a required header Postman auto-adds (e.g. `Accept`, `User-Agent`) that you dropped is the next likely culprit.

The silent bug: `response.status_code` is an `int`, and `fe.write(website + " error " + response.status_code + "\n")` raises `TypeError` for every non-200 site. But since you never consume `executor.map`'s return value (it's called on a bare line), that exception is stored in a discarded `Future` instead of being raised — so you get no traceback and no write. If none of your test sites happen to return exactly 200, `working.txt` stays empty too, matching what you're seeing even though `checker` clearly ran (it printed status codes).

Fix the type, and force exceptions to surface so this doesn't hide bugs silently:

```python
fe.write(website + " error " + str(response.status_code) + "\n")
...
list(executor.map(checker, websites))  # consuming it forces any exception to raise
```

Consuming `map`'s result (or using `submit`/`as_completed`) is good general practice — ThreadPoolExecutor swallows worker exceptions until you actually retrieve results.

This is the classic Windows `MAX_PATH` (260-character) limitation. `is_dir()` on an unresolved relative path asks Windows to combine your (evidently long) current working directory with the `../../../a/b/c` segments to locate the target; if that combined path exceeds 260 characters, the underlying stat call fails and `is_dir()` returns `False` — even though the final resolved path is short. `resolve()` collapses the `..` segments into a clean short absolute path before the OS call, so it succeeds; dropping the last path component happens to bring the (still relative) combined path under the limit too, which is why that version also works.

Fixes:

```python
p.resolve().is_dir()   # what you already found
```

or enable Windows long-path support so raw/relative paths stop hitting the limit:

```
HKLM\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\FileSystem\\LongPathsEnabled = 1
```

(reboot after setting), combined with a Python 3.6+ build that opts into long-path awareness (most modern python.org/Store installers already do).

The `for i in forcelist:` loop only appears to run once because control never gets back to it: `while robot.step(timestep) != -1:` has no `break`, so once you enter it for the first `i`, execution stays inside that `while` (and inside the `with open(...)` block) for the rest of the simulation — always reusing the first force value. `timer > 380` doesn't exit anything; there's no exit condition anywhere in the loop.

Add an explicit break once a test phase finishes, and reset state each outer iteration:

```python
for i in forcelist:
    with open(f"...force={i}...csv", 'w', encoding='UTF8') as f:
        writer = csv.writer(f)
        writer.writerow([...])
        timer = 0
        while robot.step(timestep) != -1:
            ...
            timer += 1
            if timer > 380:
                break   # returns control to the for loop for the next i
```

Also reset `arm_pos`, `wst_pos`, `fgr_pos` at the top of each `for` iteration, or each new CSV will start from leftover state from the previous force value.

For this, use pandas (or numpy's `unique`), not nested Python loops — that's exactly what makes it O(N) instead of O(N·range(M)):

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame(array, columns=['M', 'a2', 'b2', 'c2'])
counts = df.groupby('M')['M'].transform('size')
result = df[counts >= 8]
```

`groupby(...).transform('size')` computes each row's group count in one vectorized pass, replacing your `SELECT * FROM array WHERE col_1=i AND COUNT(i)>=8` pattern directly (it's the literal equivalent of a `HAVING COUNT(*) >= 8` filter). If you want to stay in pure numpy:

```python
vals, counts = np.unique(array[:, 0], return_counts=True)
keep_vals = vals[counts >= 8]
result = array[np.isin(array[:, 0], keep_vals)]
```

Both are dramatically faster than looping through the array once per possible `M` value. If it doesn't fit in memory, run the same query over the array with DuckDB (`SELECT * FROM t WHERE M IN (SELECT M FROM t GROUP BY M HAVING COUNT(*) >= 8)`), which is literally the SQL you described, without loading it all into a Python list first.

Model this as chain-resolution via a dict, not an O(n²) DataFrame scan. Build an old→new lookup once, then follow each chain to its end in Python (each chain is short, so this is effectively O(n)):

```python
mapping = dict(zip(df['old'].to_list(), df['new'].to_list()))

def resolve(code):
    seen = set()
    while code in mapping and code not in seen:
        seen.add(code)
        code = mapping[code]
    return code

df = df.with_columns(
    pl.col('old').map_elements(resolve, return_dtype=pl.Utf8).alias('latest')
)
```

This replaces your quadratic loop with O(1) dict lookups per hop, which is what actually makes it slow at scale — `set_at_idx`/row-wise mutation defeats Polars' optimizer, but a dict lookup outside the DataFrame doesn't. If you want a fully vectorized version instead, repeatedly self-join `new` back onto `old` (`df.join(df, left_on='new', right_on='old', how='left')`, taking the joined value when present) for a fixed number of rounds bounded by the longest chain, stopping once a round produces no changes.

Just filter with a list comprehension keyed on the first element — no manual searching/indexing needed:

```python
def remove_by_id(data, target_id):
    return [row for row in data if row[0] != target_id]

data = [['NS1259', 163, 8.38, 268], ['NS6969', 88, 15.7, 620],
        ['NS4722', 155, 10.02, 343], ['NS3629', 150, 5.4, 530]]

data = remove_by_id(data, 'NS6969')
```

This returns a new list containing every sublist whose first element isn't `'NS6969'`, which matches your expected output exactly. If you'd rather mutate the original list object in place instead of rebinding `data`, do `data[:] = [row for row in data if row[0] != target_id]`. If duplicate IDs are possible and you only want to remove the first match rather than all of them, use `next((i for i, row in enumerate(data) if row[0] == target_id), None)` to find the index and `del data[i]`.

QGIS bundles and runs its own separate Python interpreter — it does not share Spyder's/Anaconda's site-packages. Seeing that `pandas`/`shapely` import without error in the QGIS console doesn't rule out a version mismatch (QGIS often ships an older or differently-built shapely/pandas, e.g. a shapely build linked against a different GEOS than QGIS uses internally), which is the most common cause of code that runs in Spyder but fails in the QGIS console.

Install packages into QGIS's own Python explicitly, from the OSGeo4W shell (Windows):

```
"C:\Program Files\QGIS 3.x\bin\o4w_env.bat"
python -m pip install pandas shapely
```

or from inside the QGIS Python console itself:

```python
import subprocess, sys
subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, '-m', 'pip', 'install', 'pandas', 'shapely'])
```

Missing here: the actual traceback text (it's cut off in your post) — if it instead shows a `PyQt5` conflict, don't pip-install `PyQt5` into that same env; QGIS already provides its own build tied to its Qt runtime, and a second copy commonly crashes the console.

You don't need a temp file — pass the in-memory data as a base64 `data:` URI, since the `"url"` field accepts those directly wherever a remote URL is accepted:

```python
import base64

with open("clip.mp3", "rb") as f:
    b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

messages = [{
    "role": "user",
    "content": [
        {"type": "audio", "url": f"data:audio/mp3;base64,{b64}"},
        {"type": "text", "text": "What do you hear in this audio?"},
    ],
}]
```

If your audio/image/video is already raw in-memory bytes or an array (not read from a file at all), wrap it with `io.BytesIO(raw_bytes)` and base64-encode that instead — same approach, no disk round-trip. Some processors also accept native Python objects directly (a `PIL.Image` for images, a numpy waveform array for audio) passed under the same content-dict key instead of `"url"`; check your specific model's processor docstring, since exact accepted key names vary slightly between model families.

Pynecone (now Reflex) style props accept CSS directly, so make it responsive the same way you would with plain CSS: use relative units/flex layout instead of fixed pixel widths, plus its breakpoint-list syntax for values that should change by screen size — pass a list `[base, sm, md, lg, xl]` instead of a single value:

```python
import pynecone as pc

def index():
    return pc.box(
        pc.text("Hello"),
        width=["100%", "80%", "60%", "40%"],
        display="flex",
        flex_direction=["column", "row"],
        padding="1em",
    )
```

Each list position corresponds to a breakpoint from mobile up to desktop, so the box resizes/reflows automatically. Avoid hardcoded `width="1200px"`-style values anywhere; use `%`, `vw`/`vh`, `em`, or this breakpoint-list form throughout, and wrap your page in a flexible container (`pc.container` with `max_width` rather than a fixed `width`) so it shrinks gracefully instead of overflowing on narrow screens.

You moved `model` and the batch tensors to CUDA, but the error means some parameter *inside* the model is still on CPU — i.e., not everything got captured by `model.to("cuda")`. This happens when a submodule or parameter is created *after* `__init__`/after that `.to()` call — commonly a layer built lazily on first `forward()` call based on input shape, or a raw `torch.zeros(...)`/`nn.Parameter` constructed without specifying a device — so it never existed yet when `.to("cuda")` ran.

Check `LSTNet`'s source for any layer or tensor construction inside `forward()` rather than `__init__`. Fix by either moving that construction into `__init__` (so `.to("cuda")` covers it), or explicitly device-matching it at creation time:

```python
buf = torch.zeros(shape, device=x.device)
```

Also verify you're not loading a `state_dict` onto a second, freshly-instantiated CPU copy of the model somewhere that shadows the one you actually called `.to("cuda")` on.

IDLE and VS Code are using different current working directories, and `pandas.read_excel('book.xlsx')` resolves that relative path against the *process's* cwd, not the script's folder. VS Code's Run button/integrated terminal often uses the workspace root (or wherever the terminal happens to be) as cwd, not the folder the script lives in, while IDLE typically defaults cwd to the script's own directory — hence it "works" there.

Fix by making the path independent of cwd:

```python
import os, pandas
script_dir = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
dataframe1 = pandas.read_excel(os.path.join(script_dir, 'book.xlsx'), engine='openpyxl')
```

Alternatively, in VS Code check your run/debug config — the default Python debug configuration in `launch.json` has a `"cwd"` field; set it to `"${fileDirname}"`. Or just `cd` into the script's folder in the integrated terminal and run `python cpitest1.py` directly instead of using the editor's Run button.
